Below is a chronological overview of how paper money was made from its origins in China through its adoption in Europe and North America, with emphasis on materials, papermaking methods, printing techniques and early security features.

1. Early Chinese Experiments (7th–13th century)  
   • Tang dynasty “flying cash” (c. 650 CE) – informal credit notes, not true sovereign issues.  
   • Song dynasty Jiaozi (11th century)  
     – Paper stock: mulberry bark, hemp and rattan fibers pounded into slurry.  
     – Papermaking: mold-and-frame laid‐paper process (laid wires left faint “lines”).  
     – Printing: large woodblock plates carved in reverse; impressions made with water-based ink.  
     – Sealing & validation: red cinnabar “chop” stamps and handwritten endorsements.  
     – Coating: occasional brushing with tung-oil or wax to improve moisture resistance.  
   • Yuan dynasty “Chao” notes (13th century)  
     – Centralized Bureau of Finance operated state mills.  
     – Similar rag-fiber paper, heavier weight, more uniform sizing.  
     – Woodblock printing extended to multiple colors by separate blocks (inks in yellow, green).  
   • Ming & Qing issues (14th–19th century)  
     – Sporadic reissues of paper money on hemp/linen rag paper.  
     – Still woodblock–printed, hand-stamped seals; by late Qing some notes incorporated simple watermarks.

2. European Adoption (17th–19th century)  
   2.1 Earliest Banknotes  
     • Stockholms Banco, Sweden (1661)  
       – Handwritten notes on coarse linen rag paper, no printed ornament.  
       – Individual branches countersigned and dated by hand.  
     • Bank of England (1694 onward)  
       – Rag paper (linen–cotton blend) imported from Holland and France.  
       – Handwritten notes printed in small batches by letterpress (movable type), then signed by clerk.  
   2.2 Emergence of Security Printing  
     • Watermarks  
       – Originating in Italian papermills (13th c.), wire-patterned moulds imparted shaded designs.  
       – British banks began specifying simple watermarks (e.g. crowns) by late 18th c.  
     • Intaglio Printing (Copperplate)  
       – Late 18th c.: some provincial banks (UK, US) experimented with engraved copper plates.  
       – Allowed very fine lines, raised ink feel, harder to copy by ordinary presses.  
     • Serial Numbers & Seals  
       – Early numbering by hand-stamping; machines introduced c. 1800 for uniformity.  
       – Embossed or inked official seals added another layer against forgery.  

3. North American Practices (19th century)  
   • Pre-1862 Era (“Wildcat” & private banknotes)  
     – Each bank selected its own rag paper, sometimes watermarked with bank initials.  
     – Printing by lithography (stone) or typographic presses; vignettes often engraved on wood.  
     – Serial numbers applied by hand or mechanical numbering presses.  
   • U.S. Federal Issues & Bureau of Engraving and Printing (from 1862)  
     – Paper: 75% cotton, 25% linen rag, with embedded blue and red silk fibers.  
     – Watermark introduced mid-19th c. (eagle, numeral) via dandy-roll wire designs in cylinder mould.  
     – Printing plates: steel-faced copper for high-relief intaglio.  
     – Multi-stage printing:  
       1) Underprint (letterpress or litho) for background tints, frames and guilloché patterns.  
       2) Intaglio for portraits, vignettes, value numerals (thick, raised ink).  
       3) Seals and overprints (flat-bed presses) in contrasting colors.  
     – Final finishing: trimming, corner rounding, packaging in bundles with strap bands.

4. Key Materials & Techniques in Historical Note Production  
   A. Papermaking  
     – Fibers: primarily linen and cotton rags; hemp or mulberry bark in early Asia.  
     – Mould types: laid (wire-striped) or wove (smoother) depending on period and region.  
     – Sizing: gelatin or rosin–alum mixtures to control ink absorption.  
     – Watermarks: mould-integrated wire designs, first on flat moulds then on cylinder moulds (from late 18th c.).  
   B. Inks & Coatings  
     – Water-based carbon black or iron-gall inks for text and images.  
     – Colored pigments (ochres, vermilion, prussian blue) for underprints and seals.  
     – Protective coatings (oil, wax) used sometimes in China; seldom in later Western notes.  
   C. Printing Technologies  
     1) Woodblock – durable for large single-color runs; dominant in China until 14th c.  
     2) Movable Type/Letterpress – fine text; Europe from late 17th c.  
     3) Intaglio (Copper/Steel Engraving) – mid-18th c. onward; hallmark of high-security banknotes.  
     4) Lithography – early 19th c.; good for multi-color backgrounds but easier to forge.  
     5) (Emerging late 19th c.) Photogravure – photographic etching of images, seen in very late-period issues.  
   D. Security Devices  
     – Guilloché & lathe-work patterns: intricate geometric designs impractical to copy by hand.  
     – Serial numbering: from hand-stamps to numbering machines.  
     – Embossing & metallic threads (first tested late 19th c.).  
     – Micro-printing & chemical reagents (ink reacting to solvents) appeared only at the turn of the 20th c.

5. Organizational & Logistical Aspects  
   • State-run vs. private printing works:  
     – Many empires maintained dedicated “treasury workshops” with locked presses and bonded labor.  
     – Private bank issuers often outsourced to commercial printers under secrecy agreements.  
   • Quality control & destruction of rejects:  
     – Culling of misprints, off-spec watermarks, bad sheets; destroyed by pulping or burning to prevent misuse.  
   • Distribution & accounting:  
     – Notes issued against gold/silver reserves or government debt; serial records kept by issuing bank.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
This survey highlights how—from simple woodblock prints on hemp paper in 11th-century China to multi-stage intaglio processes on cotton-linen stock in 19th-century Europe and America—governments steadily evolved both materials and techniques to make paper money more durable and harder to counterfeit.
